questions.q: What makes enum different from interfaces, type aliases and annotations?
questions.explain: Almost all TypeScript syntax is erased. An enum is also a value, so tsc emits code that builds an object for it.
options: It is checked at runtime on every assignment
It generates JavaScript: an object that exists when the program runs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without initialisers, the first member is 0 and each next one is one higher, so Shipped is 2 and Delivered is 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A member without a value continues counting from the member before it: 61 + 1 = 62, and 91 + 1 = 92.

questions.q: tsc emits Status[Status["Paid"] = 1] = "Paid"; for a numeric member. What does this line do?
questions.explain: The inner assignment Status["Paid"] = 1 evaluates to 1, so the outer assignment is Status[1] = "Paid". That second key is the reverse mapping.
options: It stores 1 under the key "Paid", then stores "Paid" under the key 1
It creates a getter that converts between names and numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Numeric members get a reverse mapping, so PaymentStatus[1] is the name "Authorized". PaymentStatus.Captured is the number 2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object holds both directions: three names and three numeric keys. Object.keys and Object.values both see all six entries.

questions.q: How do you list only the members of a numeric enum Frequency, as numbers?
questions.explain: The values are a mix of numbers (from the name keys) and names (from the reverse mapping keys). Keeping only the numbers gives exactly one entry per member.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: String members get no reverse mapping, so the object only has the two name keys. Currency.Naira is its value, "NGN".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON gets the member values. A numeric enum becomes an unreadable number in every API response and database row; a string enum stays readable.

questions.q: With enum Currency { Naira = "NGN" } and function format(c: Currency), why is format("NGN") a compile error?
questions.explain: Unlike every other TypeScript type, string enum types are matched by name. The literal "NGN" has the same value but not the same type, so you must write Currency.Naira or convert after a check.
options: Because "NGN" is not the value of Currency.Naira
Because string enums are nominal: only the enum's own members are accepted, not equal plain strings
Because string enums only accept numbers
Because enums are erased, so Currency does not exist

questions.q: Which line compiles with enum PaymentStatus { Pending, Paid }?
questions.explain: A numeric literal that is not a member is refused, but any value of type number is accepted, because numeric enums are also used for combined bit flags. So a numeric enum parameter does not guarantee a real member.
options: const n: number = 7; const s: PaymentStatus = n;

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: The number 5 is accepted as a PaymentStatus, and the reverse mapping has no key 5, so the lookup gives undefined and ?? supplies the fallback.

questions.q: Version 1 stored StatusV1.Refunded in the database. Version 2 inserted a member. What does this print?
questions.explain: Numeric values come from member order. Inserting Disputed shifted Refunded to 3, so the stored 2 now means "Disputed". Pin every value explicitly, or store strings.

questions.q: You must keep a numeric enum whose values are stored in a database. What is the safe way to add a member?
questions.explain: Stored numbers are a contract. Explicit, never-reused values keep old rows meaning the same thing. tsc has no idea what is in your database.
options: Insert it where it reads best; TypeScript renumbers stored values
Give every member an explicit number, and give the new member a new number that was never used
Convert the enum to a const enum
Add it anywhere and run tsc, which reports conflicts

questions.q: Without isolatedModules, what does tsc emit for const enum Direction { Debit = "DR" } and const d = Direction.Debit;?
questions.explain: That is the purpose of const enum: tsc inlines each value and deletes the declaration, leaving a comment with the member's name.
options: An enum object plus const d = Direction.Debit;
No enum object, and const d = "DR" /* Direction.Debit */;
A frozen object: const Direction = Object.freeze({ Debit: "DR" })
A runtime error, because const enums cannot be compiled

questions.q: With verbatimModuleSyntax (which implies isolatedModules), how does TypeScript 7 compile a const enum?
questions.explain: Under isolatedModules, code must be translatable one file at a time, and a tool translating one file cannot see an enum's values in another file. So the enum is kept as a real object, and inlining is dropped.
options: It inlines the values, as without the option
Like a normal enum: the object is emitted and uses stay as member accesses
It refuses to compile any const enum
It converts it to a literal union

questions.q: Why can't tools such as tsx, bundlers and Node.js inline const enum values from another file?
questions.explain: Per-file translation is what makes these tools fast. To inline Direction.Debit, a tool would need the declaration from direction.ts, which it never reads.
options: Because they translate each file on its own, without reading the files it imports
Because inlining would make the code slower
Because enums are not allowed in ES modules

questions.q: What happens with const enum Priority { Low, High } and Priority[0]?
questions.explain: A const enum is designed to have no object at runtime, so reverse lookups are forbidden, even in configurations where the object happens to be emitted.
options: Compile error TS2476: a const enum member can only be accessed using a string literal

questions.q: What happens when Node.js 24 runs node status.ts on a file with an enum, without extra flags?
questions.explain: Node's type stripping only deletes types; it never generates code. An enum needs generated code, so Node refuses it. --experimental-transform-types or tsx can run it.
options: It runs, because Node understands all TypeScript
It runs, but ignores the enum
It fails with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX: enums are not supported in strip-only mode
It type-checks the file and reports type errors

questions.q: Does Node's type stripping accept a const enum?
questions.explain: Inlining would need code generation and knowledge of other files, which type stripping does neither of. Node also ignores tsconfig.json.
options: No, it is refused with the same error as a normal enum
Yes, but only string const enums

questions.q: What does the erasableSyntaxOnly compiler option do?
questions.explain: With erasableSyntaxOnly, tsc flags every construct that needs generated code (error TS1294), so code that must run under plain node is caught before it runs.
options: It erases enums automatically when compiling
It makes tsc report syntax that cannot be removed by type stripping, such as enums and parameter properties
It removes all type annotations from the output

questions.q: Which of these is allowed under erasableSyntaxOnly?
questions.explain: An as const object is plain JavaScript plus a type-only suffix. Enums, parameter properties and namespaces with code all generate JavaScript and are rejected.

questions.q: Given const PaymentStatus = { Pending: "pending", Paid: "paid" } as const;, what is (typeof PaymentStatus)[keyof typeof PaymentStatus]?
questions.explain: keyof typeof PaymentStatus is the union of the names. Indexing the object's type with every name gives the union of the values, which as const kept as literals.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you leave out as const in const Role = { Admin: "admin", Customer: "customer" };?
questions.explain: Without as const, TypeScript assumes the properties may change later and infers string for each. The derived "union" collapses to string.
options: The object is not created at runtime
The values widen to string, so the derived type is just string and accepts any text
The object becomes nominal like an enum

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An as const object has no reverse mapping, so it has exactly three values. The plain string "customer" is accepted as a Role because the derived type is a structural union.

questions.q: A status arrives from JSON as a plain string. Why is a literal union type ("pending" | "paid") easier to work with than a string enum here?
questions.explain: A union is structural: a checked "paid" is simply a "pending" | "paid". With a string enum, you also have to turn the string into Status.Paid, usually with a lookup or an assertion.
options: Because the union validates the JSON automatically
Because once the string has been checked, it already is a member of the union; no conversion to an enum member is needed
Because unions are faster at runtime
Because JSON cannot contain enum values

questions.q: What does a bare literal union type such as type Currency = "NGN" | "USD" not give you?
questions.explain: Types are erased, so the union leaves nothing at runtime. When you need the list, write an as const array or object and derive the type from it.
options: A list of the values at runtime, for a dropdown or input validation

questions.q: Where is a numeric enum a reasonable choice?
questions.explain: When the order itself carries meaning and the numbers are never stored or sent, numeric enums fit well. Values that leave the process are better as readable strings.
options: Payment statuses stored in a database and shown in an admin panel
Ordered log levels compared with <= inside one process, like LoggerLevel in @zudojs/logger
Currency codes sent to a partner bank

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: LoggerLevel is a numeric enum where lower means more severe (ERROR is 1, DEBUG is 4). With an INFO threshold, a WARN message is severe enough to be logged.
questions.code:
import { LoggerLevel, shouldLog } from "@zudojs/logger";

console.log(LoggerLevel.ERROR < LoggerLevel.DEBUG, shouldLog(LoggerLevel.INFO, LoggerLevel.WARN));

questions.q: Why should a published library avoid exporting a const enum?
questions.explain: Inlining needs the value at compile time from a declaration file, which per-file tools cannot do. TypeScript reports an error for ambient const enums under isolatedModules.
options: Because npm rejects packages with enums
Because consumers compiling with isolatedModules cannot inline it from the library's .d.ts file
Because const enums are slower than normal enums

questions.q: You replace enum PaymentStatus { Pending, Paid } with an as const object with the same member names, and a type named PaymentStatus. Which existing code breaks?
questions.explain: Member access and the type name keep working. The reverse mapping only existed on numeric enums, so reverse lookups, and any code comparing numbers, must change; tsc points at each one.
options: PaymentStatus[status] used to turn a number into a name

questions.q: During the migration, old rows store numbers and new rows store strings. How should old numbers be translated?
questions.explain: Positions change when someone reorders the object. An explicit table keeps the meaning of every old row fixed forever.
options: With an explicit table, { 0: "pending", 1: "authorized", … }, that never depends on member order

questions.q: Why write a test that compares Object.values(PaymentStatus) with a hard-coded list of strings?
questions.explain: Renaming a value compiles fine and quietly breaks every stored row. A snapshot of the values catches it in CI.
options: Because the compiler checks names, not whether the values still match the database and partner systems; the test makes any change a deliberate, reviewed decision
To check that the object is frozen

questions.q: Build options from the numeric enum: one { value, label } per member, where label is the member name. The program should print 4 and the first option.
questions.explain: Filter out the reverse-mapping entries by keeping the numbers, then use the reverse mapping deliberately to get each name.

questions.q: Replace the string enum with an as const object called Currency and a derived type of the same name, so that format(2500, "USD") compiles and Currency.Naira still works.
questions.explain: The derived type is "NGN" | "USD", which is structural, so the literal "USD" is accepted. Member access works exactly as before.

questions.q: Write isPaymentStatus(value: unknown): value is PaymentStatus using the values of the PaymentStatus object, and print the result for each input.
questions.explain: The object's values are the single source of truth for the guard. "Paid" is a member name, not a value, so it is refused.

questions.q: Finish readStatus(stored: unknown): numbers 0, 1 and 2 map to "pending", "paid" and "refunded" through an explicit table; the three strings are returned as they are; anything else returns "invalid".
questions.explain: An explicit table keeps old numbers meaning the same thing forever. LEGACY[5] is undefined, so ?? turns it into "invalid".

questions.q: Give every KycLevel member an explicit value: None = 0, Basic = 10, Enhanced = 15, Verified = 20. canTransfer must be true from Basic upwards.
questions.explain: Explicit, gapped values let you insert a level later without renumbering, and the comparison still works because the order carries meaning.

questions.q: Finish nextAction with a switch over the literal union, returning wait, send receipt and close for pending, paid and refunded.
questions.explain: A literal union gives the same exhaustiveness checking as an enum: every case returns, so no final return is needed, and a new status without a case is a compile error.

questions.q: Stored rows hold numeric statuses. Use the enum's reverse mapping to print each as NUMBER=NAME, with unknown for a number that is not a member.
questions.explain: PaymentStatus[n] reads the reverse mapping. A number that is not a member has no key, so the lookup is undefined, and ?? gives the fallback. The enum type alone would not have stopped the 9.

questions.q: Derive the type PaymentMethod from the METHODS array with (typeof METHODS)[number], write the guard isPaymentMethod, and print the valid methods from the input.
questions.explain: An as const array is the smallest enum replacement: a runtime list and, through (typeof METHODS)[number], the union type "card" | "transfer" | "ussd". The guard makes filter return PaymentMethod[].
